blocks.body:
If thirteen people are in a room, two of them were born in the same month. That is the pigeonhole principle, and it sounds too obvious to be useful. Its power lies in choosing the right pigeons and the right holes: with a clever choice, it proves the existence of structure that nobody can point to directly.

Double counting is its partner. Count one collection of objects in two different ways and set the answers equal; you get an identity, or, if one count is only an estimate, an inequality. Together they are the opening move in most extremal problems: they convert a structural question into a count that cannot be too large.

blocks.title: Pigeonhole principle
blocks.body:
If $N$ objects are placed into $k$ boxes, then some box holds at least $\lceil N/k\rceil$ objects (and some box holds at most $\lfloor N/k \rfloor$). In particular, if $N > k$, some box holds at least two objects.

If infinitely many objects are placed into finitely many boxes, some box holds infinitely many.

Suppose every box held at most $\lceil N/k\rceil - 1$ objects. Since $\lceil N/k \rceil < N/k + 1$, we have $\lceil N/k\rceil - 1 < N/k$, so the total would be less than $k \cdot N/k = N$, a contradiction. The "at most" statement is the same argument with the inequalities reversed: if every box held more than $\lfloor N/k\rfloor$, i.e. at least $\lfloor N/k \rfloor + 1 > N/k$, the total would exceed $N$. For the infinite version, a finite union of finite sets is finite.

blocks.title: Choosing the boxes
blocks.body:
The principle itself is never the hard part; the hard part is deciding what the boxes are. A good choice has two features: the number of boxes is smaller than the number of objects, and two objects in the same box automatically give what you want.

Example: among any five points in a unit square, some two are at distance at most $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$. Cut the square into four squares of side $\frac12$. Two of the five points lie in the same small square (points on a cut line can be assigned to either side), and any two points of a square of side $\frac12$ are at distance at most its diagonal, $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

Common box choices: residues modulo $n$; pieces of a geometric region; the possible values of some integer-valued quantity attached to each object (a "label"). The examples below use each of these.

blocks.title: A block sum divisible by n
blocks.body: Show that among any $n$ integers $a_1, \dots, a_n$ (in this order) there is a nonempty block of consecutive terms $a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} + \cdots + a_j$ whose sum is divisible by $n$.
blocks.solution:
Consider the $n+1$ prefix sums $S_0 = 0, S_1 = a_1, S_2 = a_1 + a_2, \dots, S_n = a_1 + \cdots + a_n$. Put them into $n$ boxes according to their remainder modulo $n$. Since $n + 1 > n$, two of them, say $S_i$ and $S_j$ with $i < j$, have the same remainder. Then
$$S_j - S_i = a_{i+1} + \cdots + a_j \equiv 0 \pmod n,$$
and the block is nonempty because $i < j$.

The bound is sharp: for $a_1 = \cdots = a_{n-1} = 1$ (only $n - 1$ terms) every block sum lies between $1$ and $n-1$, so no block works. The trick of passing to prefix sums turns "some subsum" into "two equal values", which is exactly what pigeonhole detects.

blocks.title: Two people with the same number of friends
blocks.body: At a party of $n \ge 2$ people, friendship is mutual. Show that two people have the same number of friends at the party.
blocks.solution:
Each person has between $0$ and $n-1$ friends: $n$ possible values for $n$ people, so pigeonhole does not apply directly. But the values $0$ and $n-1$ cannot both occur: a person with $n-1$ friends is friends with everyone, so nobody has $0$ friends. Hence the $n$ friend counts take at most $n - 1$ distinct values, and two people share a value.

In graph language ([[graph-basics]]): every finite simple graph with at least two vertices has two vertices of the same degree.

blocks.title: Monotone subsequences (Erdős–Szekeres)
blocks.body: Show that every sequence of $n^2 + 1$ distinct real numbers contains an increasing subsequence of length $n+1$ or a decreasing subsequence of length $n+1$. Show that $n^2$ terms are not enough.
blocks.solution:
Let the sequence be $x_1, \dots, x_{n^2+1}$. Label each term $x_i$ with $L_i$, the length of the longest increasing subsequence that starts at $x_i$. If some $L_i \ge n + 1$ we are done. Otherwise every label lies in $\{1, \dots, n\}$, and $n^2 + 1$ terms share $n$ labels, so some label is carried by at least $\lceil (n^2+1)/n\rceil = n + 1$ terms, say $x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_{n+1}}$ with $i_1 < \cdots < i_{n+1}$.

These terms form a decreasing subsequence. Indeed, if $s < t$ and $x_{i_s} < x_{i_t}$, then putting $x_{i_s}$ in front of a longest increasing subsequence starting at $x_{i_t}$ gives an increasing subsequence starting at $x_{i_s}$ of length $L_{i_t} + 1$, so $L_{i_s} > L_{i_t}$, contradicting equal labels. As the terms are distinct, $x_{i_s} > x_{i_t}$.

Sharpness: for $n = 3$, the sequence $7, 8, 9, 4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3$ has no increasing or decreasing subsequence of length $4$. An increasing subsequence stays inside one block of three, and a decreasing one takes at most one term from each block. The same construction with $n$ blocks of $n$ works in general.

blocks.title: Double counting
blocks.body:
To double count, pick a set of pairs and count it once by the first coordinate and once by the second.

A first identity: $\sum_{k=0}^{n} k\binom{n}{k} = n\,2^{n-1}$. Count pairs (committee, chair) where the committee is any subset of $n$ people and the chair is a member. Choosing the committee first: a committee of size $k$ has $k$ possible chairs, giving the left side. Choosing the chair first: $n$ ways, then any subset of the remaining $n-1$ people joins, giving $n2^{n-1}$.

The most used instance concerns graphs. A graph has vertices and edges, each edge joining two vertices; $\deg v$ is the number of edges at $v$.

blocks.title: Handshake lemma
blocks.body:
In every finite graph $G = (V, E)$,
$$\sum_{v\in V}\deg v = 2|E|.$$
Consequently the number of vertices of odd degree is even.

Count the pairs $(v, e)$ with $v \in V$, $e \in E$ and $v$ an endpoint of $e$. Grouping by $v$, vertex $v$ appears in $\deg v$ pairs, so there are $\sum_v \deg v$ pairs. Grouping by $e$, every edge has exactly two endpoints, so there are $2|E|$ pairs. The two counts are equal.

For the consequence: the sum of all degrees is even, the even degrees contribute an even amount, so the odd degrees must add up to an even number, which requires an even number of them.

blocks.title: Double counting with an inequality
blocks.body:
Often one of the two counts is exact and the other is only bounded, and the comparison gives an inequality. The classical pattern is to count small configurations, such as pairs of neighbours, and use the hypothesis to bound how often each configuration can occur. We also need one elementary inequality: for real numbers $d_1, \dots, d_n$ with mean $m$,
$$\sum_{i} d_i^2 \ge n m^2 = \frac{1}{n}\Big(\sum_i d_i\Big)^2,$$
because $\sum_i (d_i - m)^2 \ge 0$ expands to $\sum_i d_i^2 - 2m\sum_i d_i + nm^2 = \sum_i d_i^2 - nm^2$.

blocks.title: Graphs without 4-cycles (olympiad style)
blocks.body: A simple graph on $n$ vertices contains no cycle of length $4$. Prove that it has at most $\frac{n}{4}\big(1 + \sqrt{4n-3}\big)$ edges.
blocks.solution:
Call a "cherry" a pair consisting of a vertex $v$ and an unordered pair $\{u, w\}$ of distinct neighbours of $v$. Count cherries in two ways.

By the middle vertex: $v$ is the middle of $\binom{\deg v}{2}$ cherries, so there are $\sum_v \binom{\deg v}{2}$ cherries.

By the pair $\{u, w\}$: if two different vertices $v, v'$ were both adjacent to $u$ and $w$, then $u, v, w, v'$ would be a $4$-cycle. So each of the $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs is the end-pair of at most one cherry. Hence
$$\sum_{v}\binom{\deg v}{2} \le \binom{n}{2}.$$

Now let $e$ be the number of edges, so $\sum_v \deg v = 2e$ by the handshake lemma. Using $\sum_v (\deg v)^2 \ge (2e)^2/n$,
$$\sum_v \binom{\deg v}{2} = \frac12\Big(\sum_v (\deg v)^2 - \sum_v \deg v\Big) \ge \frac12\Big(\frac{4e^2}{n} - 2e\Big).$$
Combining, $\frac{2e^2}{n} - e \le \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$, i.e. $4e^2 - 2ne - n^2(n-1) \le 0$. The quadratic in $e$ has positive root $\frac{2n + \sqrt{4n^2 + 16n^2(n-1)}}{8} = \frac{n}{4}\big(1 + \sqrt{4n-3}\big)$, so $e$ is at most that.

For example, with $n = 5$ the bound is $\frac54(1 + \sqrt{17}) \approx 6.40$, so at most $6$ edges, and $6$ is achieved (two triangles sharing a vertex). The bound shows that a $4$-cycle-free graph has at most about $\frac12 n^{3/2}$ edges, far fewer than the $\binom n2$ possible: the start of [[extremal-graphs|extremal graph theory]].

blocks.body:
- Using $n$ boxes for $n$ objects: pigeonhole needs strictly more objects than boxes to force a pair (or the ceiling form $\lceil N/k\rceil$ for larger crowds).
- Choosing boxes for which "two in the same box" does not give the conclusion; check this before counting.
- Pigeonhole proves existence and does not tell you which box; do not claim more.
- In double counting both sides must count exactly the same set of pairs; a mismatch (for example ordered pairs on one side and unordered on the other) gives factors of $2$ in the wrong place.
- The ceiling is essential: $10$ objects in $3$ boxes force a box with $\lceil 10/3\rceil = 4$, not $3$.

Both principles build on [[counting]]. They are the first tools of [[extremal-graphs|extremal graph theory]] (the $4$-cycle bound is the simplest case of the Kővári–Sós–Turán theorem), of [[ramsey|Ramsey theory]] (whose basic proofs are repeated pigeonhole arguments), of [[set-systems|extremal set theory]] (double counting incidences between sets and elements), and of [[discrete-geometry|combinatorial geometry]] (pigeonhole on regions, double counting point–line incidences). In number theory the same idea gives Dirichlet's approximation theorem in [[diophantine-approx]].

1. Show that among any $7$ integers there are two whose sum or difference is divisible by $10$.
2. Show that if $51$ numbers are chosen from $\{1, 2, \dots, 100\}$, two of them are coprime, and two of them have the property that one divides the other.
3. Prove $\sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2\binom{n}{k} = n(n+1)2^{n-2}$ for $n \ge 2$ by counting committees with a chair and a secretary, who may be the same person.
4. Every vertex of a graph has degree $3$, and the graph has $150$ edges. How many vertices does it have? Can a graph have every vertex of degree $3$ and $11$ vertices?
